In [[dynamical systems theory]], an area of [[pure mathematics]], a '''Morse–Smale system''' is a smooth dynamical system whose [[non-wandering set]] consists of finitely many [[hyperbolic equilibrium point]]s and [[hyperbolic set|hyperbolic]] [[periodic orbit]]s and satisfying a transversality condition on the [[stable manifold|stable]] and unstable [[manifold]]s. Morse–Smale systems are [[structural stability|structurally stable]] and form one of the simplest and best studied classes of smooth dynamical systems. They are named after [[Marston Morse]], the creator of the [[Morse theory]], and [[Stephen Smale]], who emphasized their importance for smooth dynamics and [[algebraic topology]].

== Definition ==
Consider a smooth and [[Vector field#Complete vector fields|complete vector field]] ''X'' defined on a compact differentiable manifold ''M'' with dimension ''n''. The flow defined by this vector field is a Morse-Smale system if 

# ''X'' has only a finite number of singular points (i.e. equilibrium points of the flow), and all of them are [[Hyperbolic equilibrium point|hyperbolic equilibrium points]].
# ''X'' has only a finite number of periodic orbits, and all of them are [[hyperbolic set|hyperbolic]] [[periodic orbit]]s.
# The [[Limit set|limit sets]] of all orbits of X tends to a singular point or a periodic orbit.
# The stable and unstable manifolds of the singular points and periodic orbits intersect transversely. In other words, if <math>x_i</math> is a singular point (or periodic orbit) and <math>W_s(x_i)</math> (respectively, <math>W_u(x_i)</math>) its stable (respectively, unstable) manifold, then <math>w \in W_s(x_i) \cap W_u(x_j)</math> implies that the corresponding tangent spaces of the stable and unstable manifold satisfy <math>T_w(W_s(x_i)) + T_w(W_u(x_j)) = T_w(M)</math>.

== Examples ==
[[Image:UprightTorusFlowLines.png|thumb|right|Flow lines on an upright torus: the stable and unstable manifolds of the saddle points do not intersect transversely, so the height function does not satisfy the Morse-Smale condition.]]
[[Image:TiltedTorusFlowLines.png|thumb|right|Flow lines on a tilted torus: the height function satisfies the Morse-Smale condition.]]
* Any [[Morse function]] ''f'' on a [[compact space|compact]] [[Riemannian manifold]] ''M'' defines a gradient vector field. If one imposes the condition that the [[unstable manifold|unstable]] and [[stable manifold|stable]] [[manifold]]s of the [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical point]]s intersect transversely, then the gradient vector field and the corresponding smooth [[flow (mathematics)|flow]] form a Morse–Smale system. The finite set of [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical point]]s of ''f'' forms the non-wandering set, which consists entirely of fixed points.
* [[Gradient-like dynamical systems]] are a particular case of Morse–Smale systems.
* For Morse–Smale systems on the 2D-sphere all equilibrium points and periodical orbits are [[Hyperbolic equilibrium point|hyperbolic]]; there are no [[Separatrix (dynamical systems)|separatrice]] loops.

== Properties ==

* By [[Peixoto's theorem]], the vector field on a 2D manifold is structurally stable if and only if this field is Morse-Smale.
* Consider a Morse-Smale system defined on compact differentiable manifold ''M'' with dimension ''n'', and let the index of an equilibrium point (or a periodic orbit) be defined as the dimension of its associated unstable manifold. In Morse-Smale systems, the indices of the equilibrium points (and periodic orbits) are related with the topology of ''M'' by the Morse-Smale inequalities. Precisely, define ''m<sub>i</sub>'' as the sum of the number of equilibrium points with index ''i'' and the number of periodic orbits with indices ''i'' and ''i'' + 1, and ''b<sub>i</sub>'' as the ''i''-th [[Betti number]] of ''M''. Then the following inequalities are valid:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Smale |first=Stephen |date=1960 |title=Morse inequalities for a dynamical system |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society-new-series/volume-66/issue-1/Morse-inequalities-for-a-dynamical-system/bams/1183523416.full |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |volume=66 |issue=1 |pages=43–49|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1960-10386-2 |s2cid=41114855 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
: <math>\sum_{j=0}^i (-1)^j m_{i-j} \ge \sum_{j=0}^i (-1)^j b_{i-j}, \quad i = 0, \ldots, n</math>
